title: Shelach: forty years (Numbers 14:33–34)
hook: a year for each day of scouting; a new generation will enter

segments.voice: Yesterday Caleb had another spirit, and your line was a different spirit. Did your we can sentence get said out loud? Today, what the night of weeping costs. Day four hundred forty-nine.

Forty days of scouting. That's how long the trip into the land took: about the length of a long summer break. Forty days of walking hills, cutting grapes, sizing up walls. Then one bad night of fear. And the answer that comes back from God is a number that sounds almost impossible. Not forty days of delay. Forty years. Long enough for a toddler to become a grandparent. Long enough that most of the people standing in that camp, listening, will never see the land at all. Today: the longest detour in the Torah, and why.
screen: `FORTY DAYS OF SCOUTING.` → `ONE NIGHT OF FEAR.` → `FORTY YEARS.`

segments.voice: Numbers fourteen. The people have cried all night that they'd rather have died in Egypt, or in the wilderness. God answers them, in a sense, with their own words. In this wilderness, the generation that was counted, from twenty years old and up, will live out their lives. Forty days you scouted the land, the verse says, "for every day a year". Forty years in the wilderness. Except Caleb and Joshua. And then a line with a sting and a promise in it: your little ones, the children you said would be taken as prey, them I will bring in. The children the parents were afraid for become the generation that enters. Is it a punishment, or something more? Both readings are in the tradition. The text calls it bearing their iniquity. But medieval commentators like Ibn Ezra and Maimonides add another layer. People raised as slaves, they suggest, learned to bow their heads. It takes a generation raised in freedom, in the open wilderness, eating manna, to have the courage to go up. Change on that scale doesn't happen in forty days. And the very next morning, the people try anyway: we'll go up now, they say. Moses warns them that God isn't with them in it. They go, and they're beaten back. You can't shortcut the forty years by a burst of nerve. The Talmud adds that this night of weeping fell on the ninth of Av, which later became the saddest day of the Jewish calendar.
screen: `FOR EVERY DAY A YEAR.` · `YOUR LITTLE ONES WILL ENTER.` · `A GENERATION RAISED FREE.` · `THE NEXT MORNING'S SHORTCUT FAILS.` · then, large: `CHANGE TAKES A GENERATION.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: accept one slow road. Breathe, and think of a change you want that keeps not arriving: a habit, a family pattern, a community, yourself. Notice the part of you that wants it in forty days. Then picture it taking years, and you still walking toward it. Not giving up; walking. Ask what small daily thing belongs to the long road, the way manna fell every morning. Let it be slow. The bell holds the time.
Shelach, the scouts' portion: forty days of looking, one night of fear, and forty years for a free generation to grow up.
Your line: change takes a generation. Today, do one small thing for a slow change you won't finish this year, and do it anyway. Day four hundred forty-nine.

howItsDone: The forty years in the wilderness are read in Shelach each summer; the Talmud links the night of weeping after the scouts' report to the ninth of Av, the fast day that mourns the destruction of the Temples.

original.note: Hebrew: forty years. a year for each day of scouting.

trapdoor: what you thought: forty years in the desert was a punishment, full stop.
what it means: the text calls it bearing iniquity, and it's also how a generation raised in freedom grows up.
what a scholar hears: Ibn Ezra and Maimonides suggest a people raised in slavery needed a new generation to find courage; the Talmud ties the night of weeping to the ninth of Av.

sources.ref: Ibn Ezra on Exodus 14:13; Maimonides, Guide for the Perplexed III:32

notes: 'for every day a year' from JPS 1917 Numbers 14:34, from memory; confirm.

Ibn Ezra (on Exodus 14:13) and Maimonides (Guide III:32) on a slave generation lacking courage: these comments are attached to the Exodus route and wilderness wandering generally; confirm they fairly support the script's use here.
Taanit 29a links the night of weeping to the ninth of Av; the script doesn't quote the Talmud's harsh line ('you wept for nothing...'). Confirm.
Whether the Levites were included in the decree is debated; the script says 'the generation that was counted, from twenty years old and up'.
